neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert. Mood: euthymic by patient report. His son reports he is 'not manic, not depressed — this is something completely different.' Notable: patient shows word-for-word repetition of a childhood story 3 times during the 20-minute visit.

neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ symmetric. No Babinski. Bilateral palmomental reflexes present.

Perseverative repetition of the exact same story verbatim was observed during the visit. He takes lithium and has CKD stage 2 (eGFR 64), which reduces lithium clearance; lithium level and renal function warrant checking.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive cognitive and behavioral changes in known bipolar patient — 16 months (son's report differs from patient's self-assessment)
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. E is a 66-year-old retired architect with a 20-year history of bipolar disorder type I (well-controlled on lithium for 20 years) who presents with his son for evaluation of progressive behavioral and cognitive changes. His son, who visits weekly and is familiar with his father's bipolar episodes, specifically states: 'this is NOT a mood episode — he's not manic, he's not depressed, this is different.' Over the past 16 months, his father has begun repeating verbatim the same stories from childhood in virtually every conversation — the same three anecdotes, word for word, regardless of whether they are contextually appropriate. He has lost interest in architecture and design, which defined his entire career and retirement. He no longer visits his former colleagues or attends architecture events he previously attended religiously. He has made increasingly impulsive small purchases — nothing major, but he bought 30 identical coffee mugs because they were 'on sale,' which his son found bizarre. His hygiene has declined. He has become socially withdrawn, showing little response when his grandchildren call. He does not recognize these changes in himself. The bipolar disorder has been stable — his last hospitalization was 12 years ago, and his mood has been euthymic by both patient and caregiver reports throughout this period. He has coronary artery disease (status post stenting 8 years ago) and type 2 diabetes. He has CKD stage 2 with eGFR 64, which reduces lithium clearance. His vascular risk factors include coronary artery disease and type 2 diabetes. A distinctive feature is the verbatim repetition of the same stories (echolalia-like perseveration).

findings.finding: Markedly impaired. Poor performance on set-shifting (Trail Making Test B), abstraction/similarities, and response inhibition; perseverative errors on Wisconsin-style sorting. Pattern consistent with dorsolateral and orbitofrontal dysfunction.
Reduced letter (phonemic) fluency out of proportion to category fluency — a frontal/executive signature rather than a semantic-store deficit.

Impaired emotion recognition (Ekman faces) and deficits on theory-of-mind / faux-pas tasks, with reduced affective empathy on the Interpersonal Reactivity Index — supports the bvFTD social-cognitive phenotype.
Relatively spared. Encoding and free recall reduced in a dysexecutive (retrieval) pattern, but recognition and cued recall are comparatively preserved.
Preserved. Copy of complex figure and clock contour intact; errors, when present, reflect poor planning rather than a perceptual or constructional deficit.
Fluent with intact single-word comprehension and confrontation naming largely preserved; no agrammatism or semantic loss — argues against a primary progressive aphasia variant.
Reduced insight (anosognosia), stimulus-bound responses, and reduced concern for test performance noted during the session.
Euthymic by report; no manic or depressive features at testing. Word-for-word story repetition observed during the session reflects perseveration.

quantitative_data.MoCA: 21/30 (executive tasks severely impaired: Trails B 0/1, letter fluency 4 F-words/min; delayed recall 3/5; naming 2/3)
quantitative_data.interpretation_summary: Frontal/dysexecutive and social-cognition profile with relative sparing of episodic memory (recognition) and visuospatial function

specialized_test.impression: Neuropsychological profile shows a predominant frontal-executive and social-cognition impairment with relative sparing of episodic memory (preserved recognition) and visuospatial/constructional function. The dissociation between impaired executive/social-cognitive performance and preserved memory and visuospatial domains points to selective dysfunction of anterior (frontal-network) cortices
recommended_actions: Correlate with structural and, where indicated, FDG-PET imaging.

output.proposed: Reduce lithium carbonate dose from 450 mg BID to 300 mg BID given CKD stage 2 and mildly elevated level
interactions: Lithium + empagliflozin: SGLT2 inhibitors increase renal lithium clearance mildly — adjust monitoring accordingly
Lithium + NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen): NSAIDs reduce lithium clearance — AVOID NSAIDs in this patient
Lithium + ACE inhibitors/ARBs: would reduce lithium clearance — not currently prescribed but note for future
contraindications: NSAIDs absolutely contraindicated with lithium (raise lithium to toxic levels)
warnings: Lithium level 1.28 mEq/L: reduce dose and recheck in 1 week
CKD stage 2 (eGFR 64): lithium levels fluctuate more with acute kidney stress (dehydration, illness)
Even after dose reduction and level normalization, if behavioral syndrome persists, lithium toxicity is excluded as sole cause and FTD workup should continue
alternatives: After lithium dose reduction and 4-6 week follow-up: if behavioral changes persist (expected), proceed with FDG-PET and amyloid PET

Lithium_Recheck_After_Dose_Reduction.test: Lithium level (6 weeks post dose reduction)

findings.finding: Bilateral frontal hypometabolism, right slightly greater than left. Right orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex show 18-22% FDG reduction versus cerebellar reference.
Mild bilateral anterior temporal hypometabolism (10-12% reduction).
Preserved — posterior cingulate, parietal, and occipital lobes show normal FDG uptake.

output.impression: Bilateral frontotemporal hypometabolism with right frontal predominance and preserved posterior cortex — pattern consistent with frontotemporal hypometabolism. Scan performed under documented conditions of therapeutic lithium level

findings.finding: NEGATIVE — global SUVr 0.94. All neocortical regions below positivity threshold. No cortical amyloid deposition.

output.proposed: Ongoing management of bvFTD in patient with bipolar disorder on lithium
interactions: Lithium + valproate (potential alternative mood stabilizer): possible alternative to lithium given CKD; valproate may also modestly help bvFTD behavioral symptoms
Lithium: continue at reduced dose (0.9 mEq/L therapeutic) — provides mood stabilization and may have neuroprotective effects
contraindications: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil) — CONTRAINDICATED in FTD; do not use despite Alzheimer's exclusion uncertainty
Antipsychotics with high metabolic burden — avoid in patient with metabolic syndrome
warnings: Do not discontinue lithium abruptly — risk of bipolar relapse; taper if switching mood stabilizer
Low-dose SSRI (sertraline) may reduce disinhibition in bvFTD while being safe with lithium at therapeutic levels
Monitor lithium level every 3 months given CKD — dehydration from empagliflozin (SGLT2i) may lower lithium level
alternatives: Sertraline 50 mg for bvFTD behavioral symptoms
Consider referral to neuropsychiatry for complex bvFTD-bipolar co-management

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), probable, sporadic — comorbid bipolar disorder type I (stable on lithium)

differential.key_features: Long-term lithium exposure can cause cognitive blunting; lithium level and dose review are essential. Persistent symptoms after dose optimisation argue against lithium toxicity as primary cause.
Family informant explicitly states this is 'not a mood episode'; absence of typical bipolar symptomatology argues against.
Paternal bipolar disorder is not equivalent to FTD; genetic panel reasonable.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI with volumetric coronal T1 to assess frontal/anterior temporal atrophy and exclude alternative structural cause
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Bilateral frontal and/or anterior temporal atrophy in a lobar pattern with relative posterior sparing

optimal_actions.action: Order metabolic dementia panel (TSH, B12, CMP, RPR/HIV per risk) to exclude reversible mimics
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No reversible metabolic or infectious cause of cognitive decline identified

optimal_actions.action: Order comprehensive neuropsychological battery characterising executive function, social cognition, language and memory
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Frontal-executive and social-cognition deficits with relative sparing of episodic memory and visuospatial function

optimal_actions.action: Search medical literature for behavioural variant ftd vs late-life bipolar disorder
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Confirms Rascovsky 2011 criteria, FDG-PET evidence (Foster 2007), and management approach (Bang 2015)

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not indicated in the standard FTD workup once a structural MRI and FDG-PET (or amyloid PET) have characterised the lobar pattern.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; it is not indicated unless overt parkinsonism raises concern for PD, DLB, or atypical parkinsonism (PSP/CBS overlap).

sequence_constraints.reason: Exclude structural cause of focal cognitive symptoms and screen for elevated ICP before lumbar puncture.

critical_actions: Verify therapeutic lithium level; treat lithium toxicity if present, then reassess.
Coordinate with treating psychiatrist to distinguish bvFTD from mood relapse.
Apply Rascovsky 2011 bvFTD criteria explicitly (≥3 of 6 core features within 3 years) and document functional decline.
Assess and document decision-making, financial, and driving capacity given the high risk of impulsivity and impaired judgment in FTD.
Provide caregiver education, safety planning, and referral to FTD-focused support resources.
Offer genetic counselling and discuss cascade testing options if a pathogenic variant is identified or suspected.
contraindicated_actions: Do not start acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Do not start memantine: no evidence of benefit in bvFTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
key_reasoning_points: Persistent symptoms after lithium dose normalisation argue against toxicity as primary cause.
Family informant's explicit statement that symptoms differ from prior bipolar episodes carries weight in this presentation.
Imaging pattern + persistence after lithium adjustment supports primary neurodegenerative process.

red_herrings.data_point: 20-year history of bipolar disorder type I on lithium
red_herrings.intended_effect: Could mislead toward mood relapse or lithium toxicity as the explanation.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Stable lithium therapy and persistence of symptoms after dose review indicate a new neurodegenerative process superimposed on stable bipolar.

metadata.notes: Moderate bvFTD in bipolar patient on lithium with CKD. Key teaching: lithium level must be checked and normalized; behavioral syndrome persists after normalization confirming FTD; behavioral profile of FTD (perseveration, social withdrawal) differs qualitatively from bipolar episode patterns.
